A documentary is a film, video, or television program that is about real things — real events, real people, real places, or real issues. Nothing in it is invented for the purpose of entertainment. It is the opposite of fiction.

When you watch a fictional movie, actors play characters that don't exist, in situations that were written by a screenwriter. A documentary throws all of that out. Instead, it films the actual world — what really happened, who was really there, and what things really look like.
What makes a documentary different from other things

From a fictional film: A fictional film tells a made-up story. A documentary records or examines a real one.

From a news report: A news report is usually very short — a few minutes — and sticks to the basic facts of a recent event. A documentary goes much deeper. It explores a topic from multiple angles, provides background and history, includes interviews with several people, and often takes 45 minutes to several hours. It tries to give you a full, rich understanding of something.

From a textbook or article: A documentary uses the visual medium. Instead of just reading about something, you see it. You watch actual footage, hear real voices, and observe real places. This makes the learning experience far more immersive and emotional.
What you typically find inside a documentary

Most documentaries are built from a combination of these elements:

Real footage — Video recorded of actual events, places, or people as they happen or exist. This is the backbone of any documentary.

Interviews — Real people speak on camera about the topic. These might be experts (scientists, historians, doctors), eyewitnesses, survivors, participants, or ordinary people affected by the subject.

Narration — A voice (often unseen) guides you through the topic, providing context, explanation, and transitions between scenes. Sometimes the narrator is the filmmaker themselves.

Archival material — Old photographs, historical footage, newspaper clippings, maps, letters, and other documents from the past, used to show you things that couldn't be filmed today.

Re-enactments — Occasionally, when an important event was never filmed, actors may briefly recreate it. However, good documentaries clearly signal when this is happening, so the viewer is never misled into thinking they're watching real footage.
The purpose of a documentary

A documentary is made to do one or more of these things:

  • Inform and educate — to teach you something about the world you didn't know before.
  • Preserve history — to create a record of events, people, or cultures so they are not forgotten.
  • Raise awareness — to bring attention to a problem, injustice, or situation that many people are unaware of.
  • Provoke thought — to ask difficult questions and encourage the viewer to think critically about an issue.
  • Persuade — some documentaries are made with a clear agenda: the filmmaker wants you to agree with their position. These are sometimes called advocacy documentaries. (More on this below.)
Types of documentaries

Over the decades, filmmakers have developed different styles and approaches. Here are the main ones:

Expository documentary — This is the most classic and familiar type. A narrator speaks over visuals, guiding the audience through the subject in an organized, informative way. Nature documentaries narrated by David Attenborough — like Planet Earth — are the best-known example of this style. It feels like a knowledgeable guide explaining something to you.

Observational documentary (also called "fly-on-the-wall") — The filmmaker films without narrating or interfering. The camera simply watches as events unfold naturally. The idea is to show life as it really is, without the filmmaker's voice shaping your understanding. The audience draws their own conclusions. This style aims for a feeling of pure observation.

Participatory documentary — Here, the filmmaker becomes part of the story. They appear on screen, ask questions directly to people, and sometimes insert themselves into the situations they're filming. American filmmaker Michael Moore is well known for this style — he frequently appears on camera, confronting people and companies about issues like gun violence or corporate greed.

Poetic documentary — This type is less focused on facts and more focused on emotion, mood, and visual beauty. It might not have a clear narrative or even much dialogue — it creates an experience more than it delivers information.

Reflexive documentary — This style is self-aware and questions the documentary form itself. It draws attention to the fact that a filmmaker is making choices about what to show and how. It reminds the viewer that even documentaries are constructed, not just neutral windows into reality.
An important truth: documentaries are not perfectly objective

This is one of the most important things to understand about documentaries. Many people assume that because a documentary is about real things, it must be presenting the full, unbiased truth. But this is not always the case.

Every documentary is shaped by the choices of its maker:

  • What topic did they choose to cover?
  • Which people did they choose to interview?
  • What footage did they include, and what did they leave out?
  • What music is playing in the background, and how does it make you feel?
  • In what order is the information presented?

All of these choices influence how you feel about the subject. A skilled documentarian can use real footage and real facts to make you feel a certain way — without lying to you, but by emphasizing certain things and downplaying others.

This is why it's important to think critically when watching a documentary, especially one that deals with a controversial topic. Ask yourself: Whose voice is missing here? What's the other side of this story?
Documentary film vs. documentary series

A documentary can take two forms:

A documentary film is a standalone piece, typically ranging from about 45 minutes to over two hours, viewed in one sitting (in a cinema or on a screen at home).

A documentary series is a multi-episode work, where each episode covers a different aspect of the topic or a different story. You watch it over several sessions. Many of the most popular documentaries today, especially on streaming platforms like Netflix, are series.
Documentary vs. docudrama — a common confusion

A docudrama is different from a documentary. A docudrama uses professional actors to dramatize and recreate real historical events. It tells a real story, but through performance, scripted dialogue, and cinematic techniques. The result looks more like a regular film than a documentary.

A documentary, by contrast, relies on actual footage and real people — not actors playing those people.
Common subjects that documentaries cover

Documentaries can be made about virtually anything, but the most common subjects include:

  • Nature and wildlife — animals, ecosystems, oceans, and the natural world
  • History — wars, civilizations, significant events, historical figures
  • Social issues — poverty, inequality, discrimination, human rights
  • True crime — investigations into real crimes, court cases, and injustices
  • Politics and power — governments, elections, corruption, movements
  • Science and technology — space exploration, medicine, artificial intelligence
  • Environment — climate change, deforestation, pollution
  • Biography — the life of a notable or fascinating individual
  • Sports — athletes, teams, or landmark events in sports history
  • Culture and art — music, film, religion, food, fashion
Well-known examples

To make this concrete, here are some famous documentaries and what they're about:

  • Planet Earth (BBC, 2006) — A landmark nature series narrated by David Attenborough, showing the beauty and diversity of life on Earth across different environments. Expository style at its finest.
  • Making a Murderer (Netflix, 2015) — A true crime series that follows the case of Steven Avery, a Wisconsin man convicted of murder, raising serious questions about the justice system.
  • 13th (Netflix, 2016) — An examination of racial inequality in the United States, specifically looking at the prison system and how it connects to the history of slavery.
  • Free Solo (2018) — A film following rock climber Alex Honnold as he attempts to climb a nearly vertical 900-metre rock face in Yosemite, California, with no ropes.
  • Blackfish (2013) — A documentary about killer whales (orcas) kept in captivity at SeaWorld, exposing the conditions of their captivity and incidents of violence. It was so impactful it led to major policy changes.
  • Super Size Me (2004) — Filmmaker Morgan Spurlock eats only McDonald's food for 30 days and documents what happens to his body and health. A clear example of a participatory, advocacy-style documentary.
Where documentaries are found

You can watch documentaries in:

  • Cinemas — Many documentaries are released in theatres, especially award-nominated ones.
  • Streaming platforms — Netflix, Amazon Prime Video, Apple TV+, Disney+, and others produce and host large libraries of documentaries and documentary series.
  • Television channels — BBC, National Geographic, Discovery Channel, PBS (in the US), and similar channels have been a home for documentaries for decades.
  • Film festivals — Major festivals like Sundance, Tribeca, and IDFA (International Documentary Film Festival Amsterdam) are dedicated to showcasing documentary films.
In summary

A documentary is a non-fiction audiovisual work that explores the real world — real events, real people, real places, and real issues — using actual footage, interviews, narration, and archival material. Its purpose is to inform, educate, preserve, raise awareness, or persuade. It differs from fiction in that nothing is invented, and from news in that it goes much deeper. It comes in many styles — from calm, narrated nature films to confrontational, participatory social investigations — and covers almost any subject you can imagine. While it is grounded in reality, it is always shaped by the choices of the person who made it, so it should be watched with a thoughtful and critical eye.
